summary.text:
Paragraph 5.5.3 is the find. Cornwall Council paid Blackburn with Darwen 8.50% to borrow £5m for four days over the year end, and Harlow District Council paid 7.75% for a month. In the same quarter the same council lent to Lancashire, Suffolk and West Northamptonshire at 4.45% to 4.50%. That is a 400 basis point spread inside three months, in the same market, from the same lender — and by a wide margin the highest inter-authority rates anywhere in the library.

Everything else follows from an unusually strong cash position: average balances of £117m against a £178.4m loans CFR, no new borrowing at all, and reserves and working capital of £163.8m covering all but £14.6m of the borrowing requirement. The report is explicit that the high balances are capital grant received ahead of spend — Darwen Town Deal and Levelling Up.

Which is why their liability benchmark matters more than most. Balance sheet resources are forecast to fall from £163.8m to £79.4m by March 2028 as that grant is spent, taking the benchmark from £24.6m to £146.1m while borrowing amortises to £95.9m. A £50.2m gap in two years.

Every table foots. Their LOBO glossary entry is one of the few that explains the instrument's downside to members.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report that went to Audit & Governance on 23 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 26 PWLB loans for Blackburn with Darwen at a balance of £98,246,099 against the £98.3m in your Table 4. Tables 1, 2 and 4 all foot against each other, as does your liability benchmark for every forecast year — CFR £286.3m less LCC, PFI and lease debt gives the £178.4m loans CFR, less £163.8m of resources gives the £14.6m of net borrowing you state.

We wrote because of paragraph 5.5.3, which contains the two highest inter-authority rates we have seen anywhere.

Cornwall Council paid you 8.50% to borrow £5m for four days over the year end. Harlow paid 7.75% for a month. In the same quarter you lent to Lancashire, Suffolk and West Northamptonshire at 4.45% to 4.50%. That is a 400 basis point spread inside three months, in the same market, from the same lender.

For context on how far outside the normal range that sits: across everything we have read this year, the previous highest was Herefordshire lending £5m each to Bexley and Newham at 7.00% for about a month, and Swale paying Maidstone 6.25% for thirteen days. Wandsworth, which lends more into this market than anyone we have found, records a peak of 5.4%. Your 8.50% is a genuine outlier.

That is worth knowing for two reasons. The obvious one is that you were on the right side of it. The less obvious one is what it says about the market: rates like those only appear when a borrower has a hard date and no alternative, and the year end concentrates that. We track inter-authority pricing across the sector precisely because no council can see the distribution from its own trades — you see the 8.50% you got, not whether anyone else got 9%. July's PWLB lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is thin, and thin PWLB months are exactly when these spikes happen. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

The second thing, and the one with a longer fuse, is your liability benchmark. Balance sheet resources of £163.8m currently cover all but £14.6m of a £178.4m loans CFR, and your report is clear why: capital grant received ahead of spend, Darwen Town Deal and Levelling Up among it. Your own forecast then takes those resources to £79.4m by March 2028 as the grant is spent, which moves the benchmark from £24.6m to £146.1m while existing borrowing amortises from £108.3m to £95.9m. A £50.2m gap in two years and £61.5m in three.

That is a well-constructed benchmark and the arithmetic checks on every line. The point we would make is only that the timing of the gap is set by the spend profile of specific grant-funded schemes rather than by anything in the treasury function, so the thing worth watching is the drawdown rate against the curve. Ten-year certainty closed at 5.83% this afternoon on notice 314/26 and twenty-year at 6.38%, against your existing PWLB at 4.40%.

Two smaller notes. Your 5.3.4 says premiums made rescheduling uneconomic. On the DMO's curve today the position has moved — 21 of your 26 loans price below par, about £8.9m of net discount against £0.5m of premium on the other five. We're not suggesting anything follows: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. The point is that the answer changes with the curve, and it has changed since the report was written.

And your Appendix 4 glossary entry on LOBOs is one of the very few we have read that explains the instrument's downside to members honestly — the day-one lender profit, the difficulty of exiting, the refinancing risk if called. We have picked up ten LOBO calls across the sector in a few months and every one was refused or repaid, so members reading that entry are better prepared than most.

On training, four fit Blackburn with Darwen. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to 5.5.3. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice and Cash-flow forecasting & daily cash go to the £84m resource fall ahead. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
